sources: 100level/first semester/mth111/Share MTH 101 TRICKS by OTOP CONSULT-1.pdf
source_note: Source-grounded practice MCQs generated from text-bearing PDFs, DOCX and PPTX course files bundled in the repository. Image-only PDFs were skipped and no OCR was performed. Existing real questions were reused where available. Question-level topic tags are metadata; the current quiz UI does not filter by them yet.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly defines a set?
options: An unordered list of all numbers
questions.explanation: A set is a well-defined collection of objects called elements or members.

questions.text: The symbol ∈ is read as:
questions.explanation: x ∈ A means x is an element (member) of the set A.

questions.text: If y is not a member of set A, we write:
questions.explanation: The symbol ∉ means 'is not an element of'.

questions.text: The objects that belong to a set are called its:
questions.explanation: Every object in a set is called an element or member of the set.

questions.text: Sets are usually denoted by:
questions.explanation: Upper case letters such as A, B, C are used to denote sets.

questions.text: The roster (listing) method describes a set by:
options: Stating a property of its members
questions.explanation: The roster method lists the members inside braces, e.g. {1, 2, 3}.

questions.text: Using set-builder notation, the set of vowels is written as:
questions.explanation: Set-builder notation describes the set by a rule: {x : x is a vowel}.

questions.text: The months of the year that begin with the letter A are:
questions.explanation: Only April and August begin with the letter A.

questions.text: A set that contains no element is called the:
questions.explanation: The empty or null set has no elements and is denoted by ∅ or { }.

questions.text: The empty set is denoted by:
questions.explanation: The null set is written ∅ or as a pair of braces { }.

questions.text: A set with exactly one element is called a:
questions.explanation: A singleton (unit) set contains exactly one element, e.g. {2}.

questions.text: The set {February} is an example of a:
questions.explanation: It contains exactly one element, so it is a singleton set.

questions.text: The set A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} is a:
questions.explanation: The set has 6 elements, so it is a finite set.

questions.text: The set X = {1, 2, 3, ...} is:
questions.explanation: The three dots show the pattern continues without end.

questions.text: The cardinality n(A) of a set A means:
options: The number of elements in A
questions.explanation: n(A) is the cardinal number, i.e. the number of elements in A.

questions.text: If A = {2, 4, 6}, then n(A) = ?
questions.explanation: n(A) = 3 because the set contains three elements.

questions.text: The cardinality of {a, b, c, d, e} is:
questions.explanation: The set has five elements.

questions.text: If every element of B is also an element of A, then B is:
questions.explanation: B ⊆ A means every element of B is also in A.

questions.text: A proper subset of A:
options: Contains some but not all elements of A
questions.explanation: A proper subset is not equal to A; A has at least one extra element.

questions.text: Which of these is a subset of A = {1, 2, 3, 4}?
questions.explanation: Every element of {1, 3} belongs to A.

questions.text: Every set is a subset of:
questions.explanation: Every set is a subset of itself.

questions.text: The empty set is a subset of:
questions.explanation: The empty set is a subset of every set.

questions.text: Two sets A and B are equal if:
options: They have the same number of elements
They share at least one element
They are both subsets of U
They have exactly the same elements
questions.explanation: A = B when they contain exactly the same elements.

questions.text: The sets A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {3, 2, 1} are:
questions.explanation: The order of elements does not matter, so A = B.

questions.text: Sets that can be put into one-to-one correspondence are called:
questions.explanation: Equivalent sets match element for element in a one-to-one correspondence.

questions.text: The sets A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {a, b, c} are:
questions.explanation: Both have 3 elements (equivalent) but different elements (not equal).

questions.text: The family of all subsets of a set A is called the:
questions.explanation: The power set collects every subset of A.

questions.text: The power set of {x, y} is:
questions.explanation: Its 2^2 = 4 subsets are ∅, {x}, {y} and {x, y}.

questions.text: If a set X has 3 elements, its power set has:
questions.explanation: The power set of an n-element set has 2^n elements; 2^3 = 8.

questions.text: The set of all elements under consideration is the:
questions.explanation: The universal set U contains every element under consideration.

questions.text: The union A ∪ B contains:
options: Elements in A or B or both
questions.explanation: A ∪ B = {x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}.
The union collects all elements of both sets without repetition.

questions.text: The intersection A ∩ B contains:
options: Only elements in both A and B
questions.explanation: A ∩ B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}.
The only element in both sets is 3.

questions.text: Two sets with no element in common are called:
questions.explanation: Disjoint sets satisfy A ∩ B = ∅.

questions.text: The sets {1, 3, 5} and {2, 4, 6} are:
questions.explanation: They share no element, so they are disjoint.
A' contains the elements of U that are not in A: {3, 4, 5}.

questions.text: The complement of a set A contains:
options: All elements of U not in A
questions.explanation: A' = {x : x ∈ U and x ∉ A}.

questions.text: De Morgan's law states that (A ∪ B)' = ?
questions.explanation: The complement of a union is the intersection of the complements.

questions.text: The difference A − B is the set of elements:
options: In B but not in A
In A but not in B
questions.explanation: A − B = {x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B}.
Remove the elements of B from A to get {1, 2}.

questions.text: The symmetric difference A Δ B is defined as:
questions.explanation: A Δ B = (A − B) ∪ (B − A).

questions.text: The natural numbers are:
questions.explanation: N = {1, 2, 3, ...} is the set of natural (counting) numbers.

questions.text: The set of integers is denoted by the symbol:
questions.explanation: Z (from the German 'Zahlen') denotes the integers.

questions.text: Which of the following is an even number?
questions.explanation: 8 is divisible by 2 without a remainder.

questions.text: Which of the following is a prime number?
questions.explanation: 11 is divisible only by 1 and itself.

questions.text: A composite number is:
options: A natural number greater than 1 that is not prime
A number divisible only by 1 and itself
questions.explanation: Composite numbers have other factors besides 1 and themselves.

questions.text: Written as a product of prime factors, 30 = ?
questions.explanation: 30 = 2 × 3 × 5 in prime factors.

questions.text: The greatest common divisor (GCD) of 36 and 54 is:
questions.explanation: The common prime factors give 2 × 3 × 3 = 18.

questions.text: A rational number can be written as p/q where:
options: p and q are integers and q ≠ 0
p and q are integers and q = 0

questions.text: Which of the following is a rational number?
questions.explanation: 1/2 is a ratio of integers, so it is rational.

questions.text: The number √2 is:
questions.explanation: √2 cannot be written as a fraction, so it is irrational.

questions.text: The number π (pi) is:
questions.explanation: π has a non-terminating, non-repeating decimal, so it is irrational.

questions.text: The set of real numbers R is the union of:
questions.explanation: R = Q ∪ Q' (rationals and irrationals).

questions.text: On the number line, a number to the right of another number is:
questions.explanation: Numbers increase as we move to the right on the number line.

questions.text: The additive identity of the real numbers is:
The multiplicative identity of the real numbers is:
The multiplicative inverse of a (a ≠ 0) is:
The property a(b + c) = ab + ac is called the:
questions.explanation: Multiplication distributes over addition.

questions.text: The statement 2 + 3 = 3 + 2 illustrates the:
questions.explanation: a + b = b + a is the commutative law of addition.

questions.text: The value of 3² is:
The value of 2³ is:
√36 is equal to:
The interval (a, b), where a < x < b, is called:
questions.explanation: An open interval excludes its endpoints.

questions.text: A proof by mathematical induction has two steps, namely the:
questions.explanation: We prove P(1) (basis) and that P(k) implies P(k + 1) (inductive step).

questions.text: In the basis step of induction we prove that:
options: P(n) is true for all n
questions.explanation: The basis step establishes that P(1) is true.

questions.text: Mathematical induction is used to prove statements about:
questions.explanation: Induction works on propositions P(n) for positive integers n.

questions.text: In the inductive step, assuming P(k) is true, we must show that:
questions.explanation: The inductive step proves that P(k) implies P(k + 1).

questions.text: By induction, 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n equals:
questions.explanation: The formula for the sum of the first n integers is n(n + 1)/2.

questions.text: The value of 0! (zero factorial) is:
questions.explanation: By convention, 0! = 1.
